problems.stem: Which README AI-use disclosure is specific enough to be defensible for a graded prototype?
options: "Codex generated the initial flashcard component (commit a3f9); I rewrote the scoring to normalize case and authored all card content and feedback. ChatGPT was used to draft, then I revised, the alt text for Figures 1 to 3."
"AI helped a little here and there."
problems.explanation: A defensible disclosure names what tool did what, where (commit or section), and what the author then changed. Blanket statements neither inform a reader nor support integrity review.

problems.stem: Why does a README traceability matrix linking theory to screen changes belong in the repository rather than only in a separate report?
options: Because READMEs must always be long.

Because a reviewer cloning the repo can then see, at the point of the code and assets, which design principle each screen change served, keeping the disclosure and the artifact together and auditable.
Because separate reports are not allowed in this course.
Because it makes the repository look more complete.
problems.explanation: Co-locating the traceability and disclosure with the code lets any reader audit the design reasoning against the actual artifact, rather than trusting a detached document.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to write your README's AI-use disclosure for you. What is the strongest bounded use?
options: Accept whatever it writes, since it knows the right format.
Use it for the structure and headings, but fill in the specific tools, commits, and your own edits yourself, because only you know what AI actually did in this project.
Skip the disclosure since the AI wrote part of the README anyway.
Ask the AI to also guess which commits used AI.
problems.explanation: An AI cannot truthfully report its own role in your specific project. The author must supply the actual tools, locations, and edits; AI can only help with formatting.

problems.stem: A reviewer says your repository "discloses AI use but I cannot verify any of it." Which repository practice most directly fixes this?
options: Add a longer paragraph claiming the work is original.
Keep a commit history where AI-generated additions and your subsequent edits appear as separate commits, so the disclosure claims can be checked against the diff.
Delete the AI-generated commits to keep the history clean.
Move the disclosure to the bottom of the README.
problems.explanation: Verifiability comes from a commit history that lets a reviewer trace generated content and the author's revisions. Squashing or deleting that history removes the evidence the disclosure rests on.
